chapters.title: Chapter 4: Cross-Sectional Momentum - Ranking and Rotation

lessons.title: Case Study: Constructing a Simple Momentum Portfolio from Nifty 200 Stocks

children.text: Time to run the full pipeline from Lesson 3 end to end: universe, risk-adjusted ranking, skip-month convention, quarterly rebalance, equal-weighted top selections, on an illustrative 15-stock slice of a Nifty 200-style universe, spanning two rebalance dates so the rotation this chapter is named for actually shows up in the numbers.

body.text: A momentum portfolio is not a static list. It is a rule, re-applied on a schedule, that keeps rotating capital toward whatever is currently showing the strongest risk-adjusted trend, dropping names as they fade and picking up new leadership as it emerges, without anyone needing to forecast the rotation in advance.

children.text: Fifteen hypothetical stocks across sectors, ranked by 6-month risk-adjusted momentum score as of the first selection date, top 5 selected for an equal-weighted portfolio.

children.text: At the next quarterly rebalance, the formation window rolls forward and every stock is re-scored fresh. PSU Defence Co. and PSU Bank Co. accelerate further. Cement Co. and Realty Co., outside the original top 5, strengthen enough to enter it. Energy Co. and Infra Co., already the weakest two of the prior selection, fade out of the top 5 entirely.

body.text: This is cross-sectional momentum's rotation mechanism working exactly as designed. Nobody had to predict in advance that PSU and defence names would keep leading, or that Realty would accelerate into contention. The ranking process itself surfaced the change, and the two names that had already looked weakest within the prior quarter's portfolio, Energy Co. and Infra Co., were precisely the two that rotated out. This mirrors the real 2023-2024 leadership rotation into PSU, defence, and infrastructure names covered in Chapter 1's case study.

children.text: What This Case Study Does Not Prove

Two quarters of hypothetical data on a 15-stock illustrative universe is a demonstration of mechanics, not a validated strategy, the same honest caveat this course has applied to every worked example so far. This case study also ignores the transaction costs of rebalancing five positions in and out every quarter, ignores taxes on realized gains, and says nothing yet about position sizing or risk management if one of the five holdings suffers a sharp reversal on its own. Those topics, along with the rigorous, multi-year, cost-aware backtesting this small example is not, are covered later in this course.

body.text: A concentrated equal-weighted portfolio of just 5 stocks, as used here for simplicity, carries real single-stock risk that a broader top-decile selection from the full Nifty 200 would diversify away. Treat the position count in this illustration as a teaching simplification, not a recommended portfolio size.

body.title: Recompute the portfolio return
body.prompt: If Infra Co.'s Q1 holding-period return had instead been +13% rather than +3%, while every other holding's return stayed the same, what would the new equal-weighted portfolio return have been, in percent?
body.explanation: (22 + 15 + 5 + 18 + 13) / 5 = 73 / 5 = 14.6%. Swapping one holding's return from +3% to +13%, a 10 percentage point change, raises the equal-weighted average by 10/5 = 2 percentage points, from 12.6% to 14.6%.

body.title: Should the system have kept Infra Co.?
body.scenario: A colleague argues the system made a mistake dropping Infra Co., since it still had a positive return both quarters and never actually lost money.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, how would you respond to your colleague's argument?
body.modelAnswer: The system isn't designed to hold every stock that made money, it is designed to hold the stocks with the strongest risk-adjusted momentum relative to the rest of the universe at each rebalance. Infra Co. being positive both quarters doesn't matter if other stocks, Cement Co. and Realty Co. in this case, are now showing meaningfully stronger risk-adjusted trends. Capital is limited, and a cross-sectional system's entire logic is reallocating it toward the relatively strongest names at each rebalance, not holding onto anything that simply avoided losing money.

body.title: Momentum Portfolio Case Study: Core Terms

cards.definition: The process of a ranking system dropping stocks that have weakened and replacing them with stocks that have newly qualified, repeated at every rebalance.
A scheduled point in time at which a ranking system re-scores its universe and updates the portfolio's holdings accordingly.
A portfolio construction approach that allocates the same amount of capital to every selected holding, regardless of its individual rank or score.

points: Applying the full pipeline from Lesson 3, universe, risk-adjusted score, skip-month convention, quarterly rebalance, equal weighting, to an illustrative 15-stock universe produced a portfolio that outperformed a hypothetical broader benchmark in its first quarter.
The weakest two holdings in that first quarter, Energy Co. and Infra Co., were precisely the two that rotated out at the next rebalance, replaced by Cement Co. and Realty Co. as they strengthened.

This rotation mechanism requires no forecasting of which sector leads next, only a disciplined, repeated re-ranking process, mirroring the real 2023-2024 PSU and infrastructure leadership shift from Chapter 1.
A concentrated 5-stock equal-weighted portfolio carries real single-stock risk that this simplified illustration does not address.

This case study closes the chapter's toolkit: universe and metric design from Lesson 3, and a full worked rotation from formation to rebalance in this lesson, built on the academic foundations from Lessons 1 and 2.
